speaker: Other
text: Hear ye, hear ye. The Court of Appeals for the 1st District of Texas 9th Session, pursuant to Adjournment of the Goddard Safety Constitution, is shown on the floor.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Good afternoon and welcome to a virtual session of the 1st Court of Appeals. We have one case on today's docket. Case number 01-19-00302-CV. Hikam Watanabe v. Summit Path Partners, LLC, Hossein Aitomohand, A.J. Ahmed, and Edward Hua. May I have the appearance of counsel for the appellant, please?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Reginald McCamey for Appellant Hikam Watanabe.

speaker: peterkelly
text: And my understanding is that you're going to speak for 9 minutes and reserve 6 minutes for rebuttal.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: That's correct, sir. That's correct.

speaker: peterkelly
text: And for the appellees, may I have the appearance of counsel?

speaker: davidpoints
text: David Points for Appellees A.J. Ahmed, Edward Hua, E.A.B.B.C. Payne Law Firm.

speaker: kylegiacco
text: Kyle Giacco for Appellees Summit Path Partners, LLC.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Thank you very much. As soon as the clerk works his magic, you may proceed, Mr. McCamey.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Yes. May I proceed?

speaker: peterkelly
text: Yes, you may.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Oh, thank you, Judge. I'm proud to represent Mr. Watanabe, who was attacked going to the aid of an employee of one of the appellees here, Mr. Hossein Aitomohand. And the issues presented for the court or whether the court, the trial court, erred in granting summary judgment in favor of Hui and Ahmed in their individual capacities, whether equitable tolling defeats E.A.B.B.C. LLC's affirmative defense of limitations, and whether the court erred in granting summary judgment to E.A.B.B.C. on any other asserted grounds. Fourth, whether the court erred in granting summary judgment to Summit Path Partners, LLC, and whether the court erred in granting summary judgment to Hossein Aitomohand. First, I'd like to address in the record that Mr. Watanabe was not a trespasser, and I think that will take care of a lot of things. In the clerk's record at 509, page 107, line 12-19, Mr. Watanabe tells why he went to the parking lot to assist the employee of that parking lot. He says, I heard Samsung, I heard yelling, and I was just across the street, like from here to here, and I saw Samsung, the manager of Hossein, surrounded by four guys. Wait, I'm sorry, the question, there's a question. Wait, I'm sorry, the manager what? Of the self-parking, Samsung, they call him Samsung. Mr. Watanabe was going to assist the manager of the other parking lot. He was not a trespasser. He was not an interloper. He was there to assist his friend and workers, Samsung, that he worked with from time to time.

speaker: richardhightower
text: Mr. McCamby, can I ask a question? Yes. Did the plaintiff park the assailant Mr. Williams' car? Did Mr. Williams use the valet service that was there with the Knox Club, or did he park on a lot operated and run by someone else, some other business?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: It is my understanding that he parked on the lot that was run by Mr. Atmohan. That was not owned by Knox. That was leased by Atmohan from Summit Path.

speaker: richardhightower
text: And did the plaintiff use the valet service with the plaintiff's valet service, or did he just self-park his car over there?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: I'm not sure whether he self-parked his car. It was not unusual for people that went to Knox to park at the parking lot across the street. It was not an unusual activity. So I want to go through some undisputed facts. Hisham Watanabe was working for someone on the date of the incident. The record at 488, page 23, line 4 to 14. There was no verified pleading for the defense of capacity pursuant to Texas Rules of Civil Procedure 93. Summit Path leased to an entity other than EA, BBC, LLC, and that's in the clerk's record 449447. Summit Path and Hosein Atmohan had no written agreement. They only had an oral agreement that said Atmohan could use the lot for certain periods of time. That's in the record.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Let's focus on the premises liability claim. Yes. The property where the assault occurred was owned by Summit Path, correct?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Correct.

speaker: peterkelly
text: And at the time, it was under the control of Mr. Atmohan pursuant to a lease?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Not exactly. They granted Mr. Atmohan a lease for a certain period of time. Summit Path retained control. If you look at the record in the clerk's record 470 and 472, you will see that Atmohan did not have exclusive possession of the premises. He could only use it during certain hours. So Summit Path never released full control. They retained control of the premises.

speaker: peterkelly
text: It seems they controlled the premises during the daylight hours and Mr. Atmohan controlled it during the nighttime hours when the nightclub was open.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Well, that's what they have said. I think that is a disputed issue in terms of what control that they had even during the other hours. There was no written agreement. This was all oral. So this is what they said orally. There's no written agreement. There's no contract. There's no lease. And of course, to escape liability, they may be saying that, but there's nothing that says that.

speaker: peterkelly
text: So we have a property and you contend there's a fact issue about who controlled it, whether it was Summit Path or Atmohan at that particular moment.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Absolutely.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Now let's turn to Mr. Watanabe. You said that he's not a trespasser. Was he an invitee? Was he a licensee? What was his status at the time?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: He was an invitee. He had been going over to that lot from time to time. He was going over to assist the employee that was there for Atmohan. So he was not a trespasser. And I think he would be best described as an invitee going on the premises to assist someone that was on the premises in need.

speaker: peterkelly
text: For his own purposes, correct?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: No, not for his own purposes. That benefited Atmohan. It did not benefit him at all to go over there. He saw a person in need that was employed by the person that was leasing the premises at the time. So that was not for the benefit of Mr. Watanabe. He got no income from that.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Well, to be an invitee, does it have to be income to Mr. Watanabe? I think if you read the definition, Prosser and Keaton, it's anybody taking a shortcut across the property, loafers, loiterers, servants, spectators, sightseers, tourists. As long as it's not for, an invitee requires mutual benefit.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: I understand.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Right. So what benefit inured to Summit Path by Mr. Watanabe going over there?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: He was stopping a crime happening on the premises. Prior to that time, there had been 10. How does that benefit Summit Path? Because Summit Path would not be liable for any injuries to somebody that's on the premises. He was trying to stop what was going on from happening. And if he had stopped it, then Mr. Samsung would not have been injured. He would not have been injured. So that is a mutual benefit of him assisting Mr. Samsung. Mr. McKamey?

speaker: sarahbethlandau
text: Yes. That excerpt that you read at the beginning of your argument, did you present that to the district court in your response to the motion for summary judgment or motions for summary judgment?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: We did. We did, Your Honor. We did. That was presented. So that is the issue is that Summit Path never released entire control of their premises. And so they had an obligation and a duty to make sure it was safe. They knew it was hazardous there. And my time is up and I'll finish my last rebuttal. Thank you, Mr. McKamey.

speaker: davidpoints
text: Can you all hear me?

speaker: peterkelly
text: Yes, we can hear you. Please proceed.

speaker: davidpoints
text: All right. Judge, I'm going to go straight to, if you all allow, I'll go straight to the issue of the premises liability issue. On September 1st of 2017, we presented our traditional motions for summary judgment. We also presented our no evidence motion for summary judgment. Appellant never responded to our no evidence motion for summary judgment. But in that judgment, I want to make sure I go through the factors that I believe all of us were dismissed on. When I say all of us, I mean all defense were dismissed on. That's the Timberwalk factors. First, let me go through the evidence that Appellant has stated that were the issues at the time. The first one was that there was a history of violent crime in the area. He also had an expert of Mr. Bell's opinions. And he also stated that there was a lack of proper lighting and adequate security. So with that being said, there's a longstanding rule in Texas regarding Timberwalk that a person has no legal duty to protect another from the criminal acts of a third person. With that being said, we can go back to the day of question and the deposition of Mr. Watatombe. Not sure if I said that correct. But in his deposition, he states that he was working. He hears commotion across the street. He goes across the street to help Samsung, as Mr. McKinney has stated. What happens is he also, there's testimony that states that the manager, Hassamon, was not there. He left at 1.30. He saw Samsung standing there with the commotion. Mr. Williams and his acquaintances tell Samsung, let's step to the back of the parking lot to check out the car. Samsung says no. Of his own doing, Plaintiff Watatombe says, okay, I can work this out. Take me back there. So not only did he not have a manager there, the attendant manager that was working there decided, hey, I don't think this is a good thing. I'm not going to go back there with them. Watatombe goes back there with them, checks them out, they're talking, and in that time, an assault happens. Now, it's a situation where a question of lack of proper lighting and security. And there's no evidence to show that proper lighting or adequate security would have helped the situation. This was an unreasonable, you know, this was a situation that it was an unreasonable crime, and he just happened to be a victim of this crime. There's no evidence that shows that anything would have stopped this crime from happening. Secondly, is that his burden to show that had you done those things, the crime wouldn't have happened? No, it's a pretty high burden, but it's a factor to consider. And so, as I go through the other factors, there's a there's a factor as far as violent crimes that the appellant talks about. He submits that there are certain things or crime from the Harris County public records. This actually going through, let me pull this up, some of the things from the Harris County I was able to go through, for the past three years, there was not much going on as far as something that would relate to this specific incident. And as far as with Timberwalk, you have to have some kind of similarity as far as these crimes, because if you just have problems going into the area, with this specific, this specific crime happening, you just have to take a look. You have a problem, you have domestic violence here, you have an assault here. And these were all in just two instances in 2012. You have one instance in 2010 with an assault. There's a domestic violence issue in 2011. There's no specific instances of this nature that a manager should have been aware of. Lastly, we, the duty that Ahmed, EA, BBC, and they were HUA, there was no duty. As we saw, the defendant, we don't even know whose parking lot it was. The defendant was doing his job, goes across the street to the parking lot to assist someone in a commotion that happened. There's no duty that exists, as far as my, as far as the appellant, appellant, appellant, excuse me.

speaker: richardhightower
text: Mr. Boyce, can I ask a question? Yes, sir. Does it make a difference in the plaintiff's status as to whether a invitee or a trespasser that he crossed the street voluntarily not to park cars, but to inject himself into some dispute that was going on on that portion of the premises? Does that affect his status?

speaker: davidpoints
text: Not at all. And I think appellant's brief is kind of a rare hearing to, you know, kind of talk about whether this is an invitee or a trespasser issue. There's no issue whether he was an invitee or a trespasser. He brought himself to this situation. It's even, even in the deposition, he says that, hey, security, the police patrolled the area from 10 to 2.30. He's not sure what the exact time that this happened, but he's saying it's between maybe 2.30 or 2.40. Everything was on the premises. Even after the assault, Waterby came back to work. He came back to work. And the only reason he ended up quitting the job or ending the job is because he got into a dispute with one of the managers. So I believe there was a safe environment, whether he was a trespasser or an invitee. It doesn't matter. There was no duty to provide for that kind of unreasonable situation or criminal activity. So with that being said, let me also go back to the two issues that are before the premises liability regarding my appellees. You have equitable tolling. It's a situation where appellant did not name or sue the proper party. Those things could have been easily discovered in discovery. Appellant never filed a request for disclosure during that time. We didn't have to just give it straight off. It was never requested. The trial judge requested it. Also, to go back to a situation of the affirmative defense, we have until seven days before trial to submit our affirmative defense. We did that. So in our motion for summary judgment, we asked for an affirmative defense because in their individual capacities, Hua and Ahmed were not the owners of Knox nightclub. Even in addition to this, we see a situation where Mr. Watergate goes across the street to the parking lot for the premises of someone else. Mr. Hua, Mr. Edward, Mr. Ahmed had no idea that there would be this kind of attack on him. That's my time. I know I have Cal behind me, so I'll reserve my time for Cal.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Thank you, Mr. Boyd.

speaker: kylegiacco
text: Good afternoon, your honors. My name is Kyle Giacca, and I represent Summit Path. I want to answer a couple of the court's questions with a little more detail. With regard to whether it makes a difference whether Mr. Watanabe crossed the street voluntarily versus parking his car, with regard to Summit Path, absolutely. If he had parked, if he was on the premises, having parked a car there, he would have been a customer of Mr. Aitmohan, and at least as to Mr. Aitmohan would have been an invitee. Here he was on the premises, not for the benefit of either Mr. Aitmohan or Summit Path. He instead just entered the premises, and therefore he is in no way shape or form an invitee of either entity. It is our position that Summit Path had turned over control. There is evidence within the summary judgment record, there's an affidavit of our client stating the details of the agreement of turning over. There's no dispute Mr. Aitmohan was operating a self-park business that Mr. Williams had paid to be on that lot, but not Mr. Watanabe. Mr. Watanabe was crossing the street to interject himself in an argument. There was no ongoing assault. Whatever conflict had started, he then went with Mr. Williams and his friends, leaving Mr. Samsung behind. So any danger to Mr. Samsung had ended, even if his initial justification, which would not have made him an invitee, at most would have made him a licensee, if he had gone over to help someone. But once Mr. Samsung has left the picture, he stays behind, and it is just Mr. Watanabe going over and talking to Mr. Williams, who is an invitee on the premises of Mr. Aitmohan. Therefore, he is not in any way, shape, or form an invitee of Summit Path. Summit Path is not in control of the premises. It had turned it over at the time of the incident.

speaker: richardhightower
text: Can I ask you about that? The records seem to reflect that Summit Path only leased the premises, just as Kelly was saying, during the nighttime hours, but would have still retained control, let's just say, during the daylight hours. Is that correct? Yes, Your Honor. So as far as exercising control, I know one of the issues is a lack of lighting. Would they not have had control of the premises to the extent that they could have modified or increased the lighting on the premises?

speaker: kylegiacco
text: Theoretically, Your Honor, yes, though their duty to provide security would only have to be reasonable as to when they exercise control. If Mr. Aitmohan had a duty to provide security to his invitees during when he controlled, the issue of lighting would fall on him. But here, all of that is irrelevant. I did want to address Justice Landau's question because the issue of whether the security would have benefited Mr. Watanabe is absolutely relevant under Texas Supreme Court precedent. Western Investment v. Arena, 162 Southwest 3rd, 547, is in our brief, involved the sexual assault of a minor in an apartment complex. The resident, the person who conducted the assault was a resident. They said in that case, there was no evidence that increased security would have prevented or caused, prevented the accident. There's no evidence of proximate cause, which is one of the prongs that we've raised in our summary judgment. Here, Mr. Williams is absolutely on the premises for right. There's no evidence that the lighting would make any difference. Mr. Watanabe was perfectly aware Mr. Williams was there. He was talking to him. There's no evidence in the record to show how more lighting would have affected anything. No evidence in the record to show how increased security. Everyone, particularly Mr. Watanabe, was surprised by this attack. No security. There's no evidence in the record to show that security would have made any difference whatsoever. That was their burden and it's stated explicitly in Western Investment where they specifically held and sustained a summary judgment because there was no evidence increased lighting would have prevented the crime. That was the specific holding of the case. In addition, with regard to the timber walk factors, there is no evidence that this was a foreseeable crime because while they put on an affidavit, an expert that said this was quote unquote a high crime area, he did no analysis to do the factors regarding similarity or proximity. The crimes they looked at were up to more than a mile away. He doesn't delineate which crimes he's looking at and there are no similar crimes to effectively is an argument of some sort where someone were there interacting. This is not a robbery. This is not an assault of an unknown person. This is an interaction between Mr. Watanabe and another person who I guess escalated. We don't know all the details, but that's not a foreseeable crime. He is not a foreseeable victim. He is not a client. He has interjected himself into the situation. To the extent he justifies it, that's fine, but certainly that situation with regard to Mr. Samson had ceased. He's the one who chose to go over and I'm not making a comparative fault argument. What I'm saying is his status on the property at that point is not to the benefit of anyone of my clients or Mr. Mahan who was actually in control of the premises.

speaker: sarahbethlandau
text: How does the evolution of the situation work here? It sounds like he at least initially approached to help somebody who was working for the renter and then you're saying that as the situation evolved, he was no longer helping.

speaker: kylegiacco
text: With regard to the status, I would say the situation, the way the evolution is, you look at the purpose that the person has entered the property or is on the property and you can cease to be an invitee if the reason why you're there has changed. He wasn't an invitee to begin with. I think involuntary crossing over at most would have made him a licensee and I'm not even sure that would be the case, but assuming he was even a licensee, once he's not going over for the benefit of someone who has a right to be there, he is just on the premises as a trespasser. He's not there for anyone's benefit. I would also like to point out in Del Lago, to the extent that this was an escalating situation, if someone tried to make an analogy to Del Lago, they had to show actual knowledge of an escalating situation. The evidence is quite clear that my clients were not present and had no knowledge of whatever situation occurred. I am out of time. Does the court have any other additional questions?

speaker: peterkelly
text: No further questions. Thank you, Mr. Chacko.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Yes, I'd like to just talk about a few issues. First, Justice Landau, if you look at the record, the clerk's record at 510, you will see how it progressed. Page 110, he says during his deposition, they were really mad, really mad, really mad. They asked Samsung to follow them and he said no. I said, you know, guys, can you just show me the car? I might help you. We're going to fix the owners, the owner club and Hosin. They can fix that for you, so no worries. I took him away from him because they were really, I mean, the way how they were talking and the way they were mad, I mean, they were like, they were, so he was taking them away from Hosin's employee, assisting this person and, you know, no benefit to him. Now, the question of whether they should have knowledge, whether Summit Path should have knowledge. Summit Path itself acknowledged in the record at 474 and 481 at least 10 similar types of crimes in the three years prior to Watanabe's assault. That's in the record at 474 to 481. So they had knowledge, even though they leased it to...

speaker: peterkelly
text: Is that an unreasonable amount of crime? Excuse me? Is three assaults per year in that area of town, is that an unreasonable amount of crime?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: I think so. When you look at it, it's on that specific vicinity. It's not like a mile away or anything like this. These are crimes they admitted to. Now, Sergeant Bale, the police officer, showed many violent crime incidents in the area. So these are 10 that Summit Path were saying, hey, we know about those. So if you've got about one violent crime a quarter, then you need to do something with your lighting. And Sergeant Bale said that lighting would have helped. Contrary to what opposing counsel just said, we did provide information in the record for the trial court to know that better lighting would have helped. And some of these things were fact questions for the jury. It's a fact question between Mr. Bale and whoever the opposing counsel would want to get to say that it's not a serious issue. But those are fact questions. So I think all of the checkoffs for the landmark case, Timber Walk, are met. I think you have proximity. You have the crimes. You have similar crimes. So I think all of those are met. As far as the equitable tolling, this should not be gotcha law when people's lives are at stake. It is clear that the opposing counsel perhaps laid behind the law. They never, as required by Texas Rule of Civil Procedure 93, came forward and said, hey, verified affidavit saying we're not the right party. You should be going after a corporation, not us. And so they waited until after the statute of limitation. And so equitable tolling would allow this plaintiff to have his day in court with these facts.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Was discovery served on them or request for disclosure?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: Discovery was served on them. As I sit here, I cannot recall. They have alleged that we did not ask them for whether it was the right party or whether it was a corporation. But they never filed it. And I think you can infer that it was done to wait until the statute of limitations ran on EABBC LLC. The other thing is, I think it's a fact issue whether EABBC LLC is even a corporation, not a sham. There is no 1099s. There are no records. There's no contracts between any parties. And I think that is an issue whether they were even in they had nothing other than a corporate formation. So we don't even know if it was a solid corporation.

speaker: sarahbethlandau
text: Mr. McCamey, did you present the equitable tolling argument to the trial court?

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: I believe we did, Judge Justice. I cannot recall exactly. That's been three years, but I believe we did present that to the court.

speaker: richardhightower
text: This became a question I have kind of a procedural thing. But is the plaintiff's third amended petition the last petition that's on file? Yes, I believe it is the last petition in this case, because I don't see EABBC as being a party to this lawsuit in plaintiff's third amended petition. Okay.

speaker: reginaldmckamie
text: I just. I believe that is it's been several years since we did the case that I just can't say for sure whether that's the final one or not. I believe we did bring them in after we found out about them. But so that may not be the final petition. I'm just not sure. Okay, thank you. Thank you, Justices for your time.

speaker: peterkelly
text: Case number 011900302CV is now submitted and the first court of appeals is adjourned. Thank you for your time, gentlemen. Thank you, guys.
